analysis.one_liner: Phases out federal contracts with private prison companies and requires federal employees to run federal prisons.
analysis.headline: A bill to end federal contracts with private prison companies died in a House Judiciary subcommittee with zero cosponsors and no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Justice Department to phase out its contracts with for-profit prison companies over six to eight years, and would write into law that the core work of running federal prisons—housing, guarding, and disciplining inmates—be done by federal employees instead of contractors. It would also bar for-profit companies from running federal halfway houses, require annual inspections of every facility the Marshals Service uses, and require the Bureau of Prisons to give people leaving federal prison counseling on record expungement, jobs, treatment programs, Medicaid, food assistance, and voting.
analysis.who_benefits: People held in federal and contract prisons and their families, who would no longer be housed in facilities run for shareholder profit, and people leaving prison, who would get concrete help finding jobs, benefits, and services. Taxpayers and corrections officers would also gain as the work shifts to accountable federal employees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal inmates, their families, and corrections workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires that all core correctional services at facilities used by the Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service be performed by federal employees, after a six-year phase-out, with a narrow carve-out letting the Marshals Service use state and local government facilities [S3].
Bars the Bureau of Prisons from contracting with for-profit companies to provide or manage community confinement facilities such as halfway houses, after an eight-year phase-out [S2][S3].
Requires the Marshals Service to thoroughly inspect every facility it uses each year to make sure it meets constitutional, federal, and state standards [S3].

Requires prerelease counseling for every federal prisoner on expungement, job programs, Medicaid, food assistance, Social Security, driver's licenses, and voter registration, plus post-release notice of fines and restitution owed [S2][S3].

Directs the Attorney General to research which recidivism-reduction programs at community confinement facilities actually work and to report to Congress on the federal prison population every two years [S2].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit prison and halfway house operators, who would lose Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service contracts, and taxpayers, who would fund the shift to federal staffing and the new inspection, reporting, and reentry-counseling duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison and halfway house companies

drawbacks.text: The phase-out is slow: private contractors could keep running federal prisons for six years and halfway houses for eight years after enactment, so the industry's role would continue long into the future [S3].

In-sourcing prison operations to federal employees would likely raise federal operating costs, and an honest supporter should acknowledge that the bill offers no offsetting funding for the new inspections, reports, and reentry-counseling duties [S3].

The bill contains a drafting error: the section banning for-profit halfway houses counts its phase-out from enactment of the "Justice Not Profit Act of 2016," a bill by a different name that is never defined, which would create legal ambiguity about when the ban takes effect [S3].

Moving prisons onto the federal payroll entrenches a government staffing model; critics of public-run prisons would argue the bill replaces a contractor problem with a civil-service accountability problem rather than fixing underlying prison conditions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core promise—ending profit in federal incarceration and giving prisoners real reentry help—is significant, but its design is uneven: the six-to-eight-year phase-out would leave for-profit operators in place for years, the new duties come with no funding, and the text has a drafting error in its key prohibition. It is a direction-setting bill more than a ready-to-execute one, and it never advanced far enough to be refined.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee sent it to its crime subcommittee three weeks after introduction, and it sat there with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Representative Bonnie Watson Coleman of New Jersey introduced the bill on September 21, 2016, near the end of the 114th Congress [S1][S3].
Not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
On October 18, 2016, the committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations, the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison and halfway house companies, which kept their federal Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service contracts; the Bureau of Prisons also avoided the shift to federal staffing and the new reentry-counseling duties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison companies and their federal contracts

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out federal private prison contracts; did not attract a single cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over federal criminal law
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a crime subcommittee on October 18, 2016, and took no further action—no hearing, no markup, no floor vote—through the end of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Private prison companies (GEO Group, CoreCivic)
against.role: For-profit operators of federal contract prisons and halfway houses
against.what_they_did: Had a direct financial stake in keeping Bureau of Prisons and Marshals Service contracts and are widely reported to have lobbied against restrictions on private prisons.

sides.party_line_note: There was no vote, so no party split is recorded; the only sign of support was one Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, and the committee that let it die had a Republican majority [S4][S5].

industries.note: These companies run federal contract prisons for the Bureau of Prisons and the Marshals Service; the bill would end those contracts and require federal employees to perform core prison work. Their revenue depends on incarceration continuing, which conflicts with the public's interest in fair, humane confinement [S2][S3].
The bill bars the Bureau of Prisons from contracting with for-profit companies to provide or manage community confinement facilities, phasing out their federal role over eight years [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Corrections officers' unions and federal civil service
industries.note: The bill locks in that core correctional work be performed by federal employees, moving jobs from contractors onto the federal payroll and under public accountability [S3].
